thread.title: What's Behind Volkswagen's Recent 8%-Plus Sales Growth? SUVs - Volkswagen AG ADR VLKAY)

author: Anton Wahlman
title: What's Behind Volkswagen's Recent 8%-Plus Sales Growth? SUVs - Volkswagen AG ADR VLKAY)
text:
The recent news - according to the NY Times - that Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) has selected Volkswagen ( OTCPK:VLKAY ) ( OTCPK:VLKAF ) as its automotive partner, got me thinking: How are Volkswagen's sales numbers doing anyways? Aren't we told that Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA ), now that the Model 3 started deliveries in the second half of 2017, is putting the other automakers under pressure, sales wise?
Let's start by looking at Volkswagen's global sales in 2018, for the first four months: Volkswagen Group delivers more than 900,000 vehicles in April . As it turns out, VW's sales are up 8.1% this year. That's a huge increase, given that the overall auto market is seeing a slowdown from the huge boom in the previous few years.
How many units are we talking about in terms of VW's 8.1% growth? It represents growth from 3,336,000 units to 3,606,900 units - or 270,900 units. On an annualized basis, that's 812,700 units.
Consider that Tesla sold 103,181 cars in 2017, and while it has guided for 500,000 units in 2018, I think it will be lucky to hit 200,000. In other words, Volkswagen is set to outgrow Tesla by 4:1 in 2018 on an absolute unit growth basis. Whatever impact Tesla is having, it's not visible on Volkswagen's numbers.
Of course, Volkswagen consists of multiple brands, including Audi and Porsche. Are they all doing well, or just some of them? For the first four months of 2018, on a global basis:
Volkswagen cars: Up 7.1%
Audi: Up 8.0%
Porsche: Up 5.3%
In other words, broadly speaking, fairly even handed. Other brands such as Skoda and SEAT that are not sold in the U.S. were up a lot more, so therefore the 8.1% average is above the three brands we know best in the U.S.
In the U.S., we are mostly familiar to some extent with the huge success of Audi and Porsche. These two brands are in the top tier of their respective segments.
However, the actual Volkswagen mass market brand is not held in equally high esteem in the U.S. market. It's viewed more as a curiosity, a bit of an oddball. It never got as successful in the U.S. market as other mass-market import brands such as Toyota (NYSE: TM ), Nissan ( OTCPK:NSANY ) or Honda (NYSE: HMC ) just to pick the three most obvious ones.
All that said, how is the base Volkswagen brand doing in the U.S. market right now? So far in 2018, it is up 8.6%: Here. That's a huge increase in a market that's only up around 2% for 2018. Volkswagen is basically outperforming the U.S. market's growth rate to the tune of 4x in 2018.
So what's driving this U.S. growth for Volkswagen in 2018?

As you can see in the table above, Volkswagen's shift to SUVs in the U.S. has been dramatic over the last year: Up from 14% in 2017 to 51% in 2018. Basically, VW in the U.S. has become an SUV company. A majority of unit sales are now SUVs, as far as VW in the U.S. is concerned, up from 14% only a year ago.
One of the factors helping VW's U.S. sales in the last few months is its new warranty, which started around the middle of 2017. It's a six-year, 72,000 mile bumper-to-bumper warranty that's transferable. I'm unaware of another warranty in the market today that has those characteristics.
What's next for Volkswagen's SUV (and related) U.S. product portfolio? I would point to these four examples:
Fall 2019: A two-row version of the Atlas, which would be a slightly shorter complement.
Spring 2020: A smaller SUV sitting below the Tiguan. Volkswagen offers such smaller SUVs in Europe and Asia, but it's not clear which one the U.S. will get.
Summer 2020: ID Crozz, which is a pure EV that would compete with a notional Tesla Model Y.
2022: ID BUZZ, which is the old "hippie van" in all-electric format, and should be very similar to the other members of the ID series, as they would share the same MEB platform.
In the meantime, what's clear is this: VW Group is essentially tied for world's largest automaker with the Nissan-Renault-Mitsubishi Alliance and Toyota, at little over 10 million cars sold per year. And yet, despite being at industry-leading scale already, the VW Group is growing at a most impressive 8.1% - and its U.S. sales are now 51% SUVs. That's a big story.
